chapter: Failure in St. Louis and the Omaha bands
title: Touring with Nat Towles and the Mardi Gras
summary: Towles toured the midwest in summer, the south in winter, and played Mardi Gras in New Orleans against a creole band; jazz was a medicine for people.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: He would lead the band when he was singing his numbers, and they had quite a trick and art of using batons of doing this with, see. But you asked me how long I was with Nat Towles. I was with Nat Towles for several -- oh, I'd say at least a year, perhaps. We travelled mainly through the midwest in the summer months, and we would go south in the winter months. We played regularly, annually at the Mardi Gras in New Orleans, and we used to play what they call battle of music with another band called -- let's see, I can't think of his name. There was another -- a creole band in New Orleans that was quite good. And we used to play with them every year, and they had this celebration down there.
And jazz was very popular in the south, you know.

And people were happy. They really had good times and they -- as I said, the economic situation had no bearing on the feelings, and that's why I say jazz really acted as an anecdote to me, and as a medicine. And I think it also was medicine to people of that time.
Yes, I'm sure it was. Yes.
You know, it helped people to forget.
